Tech.title: Please Stop Making Me Opt Out of AI
Tech.content:
In early July, Meta rolled out a new feature where anyone using its AI app could tag public Instagram accounts and generate images using their likenesses. Meta’s decision to turn the feature on by default, so that Instagram users had to actively opt out, was controversial.

Multiple Instagram creators posted viral videos explaining how to opt out and expressed frustration. After three days of outcry, Meta said in a statement that “this feature missed the mark” and rolled back Instagram tagging for its AI chatbot.

“They should have given you the option to opt in rather than opt out. But I am really getting tired of these companies pushing this AI stuff on us when we don’t want to use it,” said creator Sam Sooin Yang in an Instagram video with over 3 million views. As public sentiment has continued to sour on generative AI, Silicon Valley companies have leaned into enabling these features and related settings by default.

The public reaction to Instagram’s “opt-out” default for that AI feature was notable for its swiftness. “That was a clear and immediate pushback,” says Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “Honestly, it was great to see how quickly that happened.” Three days from lights on to lights off for a generative AI feature has to be some kind of record.

Recently, I turned off the “Ask Gemini” bar in my Google Docs. It popped up at the bottom of my documents one morning and prompted me to use Google's chatbot as part of my regular writing workflow. Immediately, I started digging in the settings to disengage this feature. It's a ritual I’ve also performed an unfortunate number of times in recent years on other platforms, like Dropbox and LinkedIn.

Tech.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 Rumor Roundup: What We Know About The New Compact Flip
Tech.content:
Samsung's Galaxy Z Flip 8 could be among the new phones announced at the company's July Unpacked event on July 22. New iterations on Samsung's Galaxy Z Flip and Galaxy Z Fold phones often arrive during the summer, and it's quite likely we'll see the foldable phones debut alongside other rumored devices such as the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Glasses.

The Z Flip 8 -- which is expected to debut alongside two new book-style Z Fold 8 handsets -- would presumably go head-to-head against the recently released Motorola Razr lineup.

With the potential release date encroaching, there are already lots of rumors and purported leaks about the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8. Here's everything we know so far.

Samsung is holding its next Galaxy Unpacked event in London on July 22. Samsung

Release date and pricing

Samsung has confirmed that the company's next Unpacked event will take place on July 22 in London, starting at 9 a.m. ET/6 a.m. PT/2 p.m. BST. The reveal date's confirmation comes following several reports from Seoul Economic Daily and Korea Economic TV, with both outlets reporting the date and the location.

Samsung has not yet confirmed the Z Flip 8 or any of the other devices, but there are a few clues about when they could go on sale. Apparently Samsung in Malaysia published details about a promotional voucher for the new foldables that would only be valid between July 22 and Oct. 4. Another leak, courtesy of PhoneArena, points to a possible release date of Aug. 7, with a preorder date of July 28.

As for pricing, there have been rumors that the prices for all of Samsung's foldables will increase largely due to the rising cost of smartphone components such as memory chips. Sammyguru, for example, says that the Galaxy Z Flip 8 could start around $1,200, which is a slight increase over the $1,100 Galaxy Z Flip 7. By comparison, Motorola's similarly priced Razr Plus for 2026 had its starting price move up from $1,000 for the 2025 model to $1,100, and the highest-end Razr Ultra for 2026 went up from $1,300 to $1,500.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is rumored to have a similar design to last year's Z Flip 7. Last year's phone included a slightly larger cover screen over prior Flip phones. James Martin/CNET

Possible Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 FE

Since Samsung released a more affordable entry-level Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE last year, there is speculation that the company will repeat history and introduce a Galaxy Z Flip 8 FE as well this year. That said, we haven't heard anything about this, at least for a potential July 22 release. There are some that speculate that the Flip 8 FE could come out later in the year, perhaps before the holidays, but there's very little word about it so far. Some even say it might not appear at all.

Design differences

There doesn't seem to be too many major differences with the Galaxy Z Flip 8's overall anticipated design. Recently leaked cases appear to point to a very similar design to its predecessor, with a horizontally aligned dual-camera arrangement integrated into the external display.

Design aside, there are multiple reports that point to the Galaxy Z Flip 8 having a slimmer, lighter build. Some leaks have revealed that it will weigh around 180 grams, which is 8 grams lighter than its predecessor. Its profile is also supposedly quite slim, measuring 13.2mm when folded and 6.6mm when unfolded. That's marginally thinner than the Galaxy Z Flip 7 (which is 6.5mm when unfolded and 13.7mm when folded) but it could make a difference in everyday use.

Tipster Lanzuk (via Android Central) also says that the Flip 8 could have a "crease-less" design structure with an improved hinge that could reduce the visible crease on the main display. It could also be ever so slightly wider, with some reports speculating that its dimensions could be 166.8x75.4x6.5mm.

Otherwise, the rest of the design elements appear very similar to the Galaxy Z Flip 7. It's expected to have a 4.1-inch OLED cover display and 6.9-inch OLED main display. Both are expected to have 2,600 nits of peak brightness, HDR10 Plus support and Gorilla Glass Victus 2 protection on the cover display.

Android Headlines has seemingly obtained press images of the Flip 8 alongside the Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra, which do appear to confirm the earlier rumors. Additionally, the outlet says that the Flip 8 will be available in an online-exclusive mint color that won't be available elsewhere.

The cameras on the Z Flip 8 are also presumed to be similar to the Z Flip 7's cameras. James Martin/CNET

Camera

As far as the camera specs go, the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8's features look virtually unchanged from the Galaxy Z Flip 7. It's expected to have a 50-megapixel main camera, a 12-megapixel ultrawide camera, plus a 10-megapixel selfie camera on the front. It's also expected to support up to 4K 60fps video recording.

Battery, performance and specs

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 might not see much of a battery improvement over its predecessor. It's expected to have a 4,300-mAh battery along with the same 25W wired charging speeds as the Galaxy Z Flip 7. There's a rumor that it could have 45W charging speeds, but the sourcing on this doesn't seem to be particularly strong, as it appears to contradict regulatory filings.

According to Samsung's FCC filings, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 is expected to ship with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in the US. Internationally, however, it's expected to ship with the Exynos 2600 chip, which fits with the company's dual-chip strategy in the past. The Z Flip 8 is also expected to have 12GB of RAM and storage options that start at 256GB.

Watch this: Samsung Galaxy S27 Pro Could Be a Mini Ultra 05:44

Is this the Flip's swan song?

If you've never purchased a Galaxy Z Flip, the Flip 8 might be your last chance to do so. According to Fireuniverse8 on X (via Sammobile), the Galaxy Z Flip 8 will be the last Galaxy Z Flip phone. The reasoning is that Samsung wants to focus more on the Fold series rather than the Flip. Seeing as Apple could release a folding iPhone that mimics the Fold's book-style design, Samsung could view the book-style design as more lucrative.

Tech.title: How to Opt Out of AI Chatbots Collecting Your Data for Training Purposes
Tech.content:
AI chatbots are everywhere, and people are leaning on them more than ever. You can use them to generate images, videos and even vibe-code apps and games. It's easy to get lost while playing around with them.

But not everyone is talking to chatbots in a lighthearted way. Some people are using them for therapy, as AI companions and to address their health concerns. Not only is that data being stored, but it can (and likely will) be used to train AI models further -- unless you do something about it.

By default, most AI chatbots and other AI tools have a setting that allows the company to use your data to train AI models, and all it does it take some tinkering in the settings to turn it off. And if you want to go even further, you can delete all of your previous conversations.

There are privacy concerns galore about AI generally, but since chatbots are the gateway to AI for most people, it's a glaring sore spot. In order to take back your data, you'll need to do one or two things, and that's opt out of having your data used for AI training purposes and delete the data that's there to be trained on for the future.

If your data has already been used to train an AI model, there's no undo option here, so being preemptive is your best bet.

Gemini

You'll need to turn off a few settings in your Google account and in Gemini to prevent your data from being used to train AI models.

Google

Go to myactivity.google.com

Click Web & App Activity and turn it off.

Turning off Web & App Activity will prevent your new searches, location and other data from being recorded to your Google account and used for AI training. However, turning this off does not delete the existing activity already on your account. You'll still need to click the delete button on the same page and select to delete your data from either all time or your specified range.

Gemini

Gemini has its own settings that you'll need to disable in order to prevent Google from using your data for model training:

Log in to Gemini

Click the Settings cog

cog Click Activity

Click the drop-down and set it to Off.

Similarly, you'll also need to manually delete the existing Gemini activity (your conversations) by clicking the delete button and selecting a time range.

Claude

If you're looking to remove your data or prevent Anthropic from using your data in Claude, it's a little more straightforward.

Change Model Improvement settings:

Log in to your Claude account

Click your profile icon

Click Settings

Click Privacy

Set the toggle for Help improve our AI models to off.

While you're here, you might also want to toggle the Location metadata off for good measure.

Deleting your conversations in Claude is also easy:

Log in to your Claude account

Click Chats on the left sidebar

on the left sidebar Click Select Chats

Click Select all

Click Delete.

Per Anthropic's privacy policy, deleted chats are stored for up to 30 days in its back-end systems. If you've previously allowed Anthropic to use your data, and you turn the setting off, new and existing chats won't be used to train models going forward, but your data will be used in training that is in progress and won't be removed from models that have already been trained.

ChatGPT

ChatGPT is the world's most-used chatbot. If you've been using it for a while without adjusting your settings, you've probably given OpenAI a lot of data.

Turn off model improvement in ChatGPT:

Log in to your ChatGPT account

Click your profile icon

Click Settings

Click Data controls

Click improve the model for everyone

Switch the toggle to improve the model for everyone off.

This pop-up menu contains two additional settings to include your audio and video recordings, but toggling the main switch at the top will disable both of these settings.

To delete all of your chats, there's a dedicated button within the Data controls menu to do this. Like Anthropic's policy, OpenAI also stores deleted chats for up to 30 days.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET's parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Meta

The TL;DR for trying to get Meta to stop using your data to train its AI is that there's no guarantee. There's no elegant solution, and you'll have to submit a form, which Meta may take action on.

Making your profiles private and limiting your posts will shield you the most from AI training. Or you can just delete your Instagram and Facebook profiles.

Instagram users looking to get away from the fact that others can reuse their own media can opt out to avoid the deepfake apocalypse.

Aside from that, all else you can do is mute Meta AI.

I was unable to find the specific setting to get Meta to stop using your data, and Meta did not respond to a request for comment when asked for a guaranteed way to opt-out of AI model training.

Grok

It's almost surprising that Grok will allow you to turn off AI model training on X, but you can. Here's how.

Log in to your X account

Click the More button

button Click Settings and privacy

Click Privacy and safety

Click Grok & Third-Party Collaborators.

Uncheck the box next to "Allow your public data as well as your interactions, inputs, and results with Grok and XAI to be used for training and fine-tuning."

While you're at it, you might want to uncheck Allow X to personalize your experience with Grok and Allow Grok to remember your conversation history. You can also choose to delete your conversation history with Grok in this menu.

There are plenty of other AI tools that you may need to do this for if you're a habitual user. We'll continue to add to them here over time. The settings may be a bit obscured and hard to find, but if the option is there, you'll typically find it in the data or privacy settings of the selected chatbot.

Tech.title: Bigger Scares: Home Depot's 12-Foot Skeleton Is a Halloween Hit and Now It Can Talk, Too
Tech.content:
Five years on, Skelly remains a firm favorite for Halloween haunts. Released as part of Home Depot's Halloween decor, the mammoth skeleton affectionately referred to as Skelly stands 12 feet tall and has gone viral multiple times, selling out every time new stock is released.

Home Depot is launching its 2026 Halloween collection today, July 16, with plenty of animatronics and other Halloween gear that are sure to get you hyped for the holiday, including an updated Skelly.

This year, the fan favorite is getting a refresh, with app-enabled upgrades that let you customize this spooky giant to your macabre heart's content. You'll control head and mouth movements with servo motors and speak through the animatronic in real time via Bluetooth, making it an interactive highlight for trick-or-treaters.

Additionally, you can record up to 30 sounds for Skelly. Plus, you can now choose from 20 different LCD effects. That includes options like heart eyes -- which could be fun for Valentine's Day -- along with other exciting presets so you can keep Skelly around your yard year-round.

This new servo edition of Skelly costs $379 and is only available online. It's likely to sell out fast, so be sure to lock in your order soon.

Alternatives you might like

Don't need these extras? You'll be able to get the original Skelly for its original price of $299 instead. Or shop Home Depot's entire Halloween collection for more options.

Tech.title: 'Power: Origins': See Young Ghost, Tommy and Kanan in First-Look Trailer
Tech.content:
As Power Book III: Raising Kanan is getting ready to wrap its five-season story this summer, Starz is treating fans to a taste of what's to come for its next prequel spinoff in the Power franchise, Power: Origins. A new teaser trailer and first-look photos dropped on Thursday, showing the dynamic duo of James "Ghost" St. Patrick and Tommy Egan as teens looking to make their mark in the streets of New York City.

Young Ghost is played by Spence Moore, with Charlie Mann as Tommy and MeKai Curtis reprising his role as Kanan Stark. In the original Power series, which ran for six seasons from 2014 to 2020, Omari Hardwick originated the role of Ghost, and Joseph Sikora played his partner-turned-frenemy, Tommy, with Curtis "50 Cent" Jackson as the infamous killer, Kanan.

A first-look photo of Ghost and Tommy in Power: Origins starring Spence Moore and Charlie Mann. Starz

The new prequel, currently in production, will explore the fan-favorite characters in their younger years as friends who got into the drug business under Kanan's tutelage. Other cast members joining the series include Hill Harper, Nadia Dajani (reprising her role as Teresa Boselli), Kelly McCreary, Damon Gupton and Tonya Pinkins (playing Ghost's grandmother). Jason Dirden is back as Traymont Stinson, a character in Raising Kanan, and Jennifer Ferrin will star as Tommy's mom, Kate Egan.

Co-created by Sascha Penn and Power creator Courtney Kemp, Power: Origins will be the fourth spinoff in the entire franchise. All series, including Power, Power Book II: Ghost, Power Book III: Raising Kanan and Power Book IV: Force, can be streamed on Starz.

Tech.title: Google Renames NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook
Tech.content:
NotebookLM is one of the best AI tools available, and it's been renamed the Gemini Notebook to bring it in line with the rest of Google's Gemini AI suite, the tech giant announced in a blog post on Thursday. Despite the name change and further integration into more Google products in the future, it'll continue as a standalone tool.

Originally launched as an experiment called Project Tailwind in 2023, Gemini Notebook has since been used by over 30 million people and 600,000 organizations, according to the blog post. The project turned into what's possibly the best AI product the tech giant has produced so far.

Gemini Notebook is a research assistant that can help you make sense of your messiest notes or other sources. It's great as a learning tool, but can be used in a variety of ways. What sets it apart from other AI tools is that it only analyzes the sources you feed it (web pages, PDFs, audio files, etc.) and won't search the internet for an answer if the sources don't contain one. For example, if you upload a document about math and then ask it about the biology of dolphins, it'll reply that, based on your sources, it doesn't have the answer.

As a part of the rebranding, Google has given the Gemini Notebook some serious under-the-hood upgrades. Google started rolling out an update last month that gives each Notebook a secure cloud computer, enabling the Gemini Notebook to natively write and execute code. This can allow for more in-depth data analysis of your sources. The update also introduced new output formats, including .json and Microsoft PowerPoint (.pptx) files.

These updates are available starting Thursday for Google AI Ultra users and Workspace business customers with AI Ultra Access and AI Expanded Access. AI Pro users on the web will gain access in the coming weeks.

Google has been adding new features to the Gemini Notebook since day one, and it's become an incredibly robust tool since. Notebooks now sync directly with Google Drive, and you can even create Notebooks directly from the Gemini App. Google says Notebooks will soon be coming to AI Mode in Search, too.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11 Rumor Roundup: New Colors, Higher Prices and Lots of Leaks
Tech.content:
It's time once again for Google to reveal its next wave of Pixel phones. The company has sent out invitations for a Made by Google event that will take place on Aug. 12 in New York at 6 p.m. ET, where it will likely unveil a new Pixel 11 series along with a potential Pixel Watch 5.

Since the event is nearly upon us, there is a plethora of rumors, speculation and leaks about what Google plans to announce. At the very least, we're expecting updates to the entire Pixel lineup -- we'll probably see the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL and a Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Google is also expected to announce Android features that are unique to the Pixel 11, at least initially, to help it stand apart from the competition. The Pixel 11 lineup is shaping up to be a showcase for Google's AI initiatives, for example, so we expect that to be a big focus at the event.

Here's everything we know about the Pixel 11 series so far.

The Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Release Date and pricing

Since the Google event will take place on Aug. 12, the Pixel 11 series will likely be available a few weeks after that. Last year, the Pixel 10 lineup dropped in late August, while the Pro Fold arrived in October. The same could repeat this year.

It appears that the Pixel 11's prices will be higher across the board, but for different reasons. Android Authority has apparently leaked some deleted Amazon listings that confirm an earlier rumor from Deallabs that Google will drop the 128GB storage model from the Pixel 11 lineup. That, of course, raises the starting price to that of the 256GB model across the series.

The deleted Amazon listings show that the Pixel 11's price starts at $899, which is the same as the comparable 256GB Pixel 10. The Pixel 11 Pro's price appears to start at $1,099, which is the same as the comparable 256GB Pixel 11 Pro. Interestingly, the 256GB Pixel 11 Pro comes with 12GB of RAM while higher configurations come with 16GB of RAM.

But premium Pixel models, such as the Pixel 11 Pro XL and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, will have a price hike beyond that, likely due to the current memory shortage crisis. The aforementioned deleted Amazon listings, which Droid Life also managed to capture, show that the Pixel 11 Pro XL and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold will start at $1,299 and $1,899 respectively. That's $100 more than their Pixel 10 predecessors.

Like with the 11 Pro, the 256GB Pixel 11 Pro XL appears to ship with 12GB of RAM while higher configurations come with 16GB of RAM.

This is in line with earlier speculation that the Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold will be 100 euros more expensive than their Pixel 10 counterparts.

The Pixel 11 is presumed to have a simlar design to the Pixel 10 (seen here), but with a new Pixel Glow feature. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Design differences

So far, leaks have shown the Pixel 11 phones to be practically identical to their predecessors. That means a 6.3-inch display on the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro, a 6.8-inch display with the Pro XL and a 6.4-inch outer display on the Pro Fold (though the leaked Amazon listing seems to show a 6.5-inch outer display instead). Android Headlines did find leaked CAD images that appear to point to the Pixel 11 having thinner bezels and an all-black camera bar, but overall the changes seem very minor.

The biggest change seems to be something called the "Pixel Glow," which appears to be an LED array outlining the Pixel's cameras. According to 9to5Google, the Pixel Glow will use "subtle light and color on the back of your device to inform you of important activity when it's face down." It sounds like a fancy notification LED that'll show you the type of notification you receive while the phone is face down.

Apparently this feature has already been teased at I/O (via Android Central) though it could also be simply an AI-generated image meant to show off Gemini Omni's capabilities. There are also supposedly some Pixel 11 cases with a wider camera cutout in order to accommodate the new LED array, which add credence to the Pixel Glow rumor.

According to some leaks, the Pixel 11 will ship in these colors: Light sterling (gray), midnight haze (black), fuschia (pink) and moss (green). The other models will apparently be available in midnight haze, light fog (white), dune (pink) and pine (green) depending on storage capacity.

The aforementioned leaked Amazon listing, however, shows that the Pixel 11 will be available in frost, pistachio, hibiscus and obsidian. It also shows the 11 Pro and Pro XL in canyon and obsidian, and the 11 Pro Fold in olive and obsidian.

The Pixel 11 phones may be getting new camera upgrades. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Rumored specs, battery and performance

According to insider Mystic Leaks (via Android Authority), the Pixel 11 is rumored to have a 50-megapixel sensor, which is an upgrade over the Pixel 10's 48-megapixel sensor. Though this might seem like just a 2-megapixel difference, this brings the base Pixel much more in line with the Pro-level Pixels, providing higher resolution and greater zoom versatility. All the Pixel 11 phones appear to have 13-megapixel front-facing cameras

Interestingly, Mystic Leaks also says that the base Pixel 11 could only have 8GB of RAM rather than 12GB. They say that there might be a version that has 12GB of RAM, but it could be more expensive. This is very different from the leaked Amazon listings that show the Pixel 11 with 12GB of RAM across the board.

The leaked Amazon listings appear to show that the Pixel 11 will be available in 256GB and 512GB configurations while the Pixel 11 Pro, Pro XL and Pro Fold will be available in 256GB, 512GB and 1TB configurations. As mentioned earlier, there also seems to be a RAM split with the Pro and Pro XL, with the 256GB versions of those shipping with 12GB of RAM while the higher storage variants would ship with 16GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold seemingly has 16GB of RAM across its configurations.

The new Pixel 11 phones are expected to ship with a 2nm upgrade for Google's Tensor G6 chipset, which theoretically points to better power efficiency. Google is also apparently switching on Samsung Exynos modems to MediaTek M90 modems, as shown in this FCC filing for the Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

The aforementioned leaked Amazon listing shows the battery capacities for the Pixel 11 lineup as follows: The Pixel 11 will apparently have a 4,985-mAh battery, the Pixel 11 Pro is shown with a 4,850-mAh battery, the Pixel 11 Pro XL with a 5,115-mAh battery and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold seems to have a 4,750-mAh battery.

We'll continue to update this roundup as we hear more about the Pixel 11 series, leading up to the Made by Google event on Aug. 12.

Tech.title: US Sanctions First VPN in Crackdown on Ransomware Criminals
Tech.content:
The US Department of the Treasury this week sanctioned First VPN Service, saying it enabled cybercriminals to launch ransomware attacks against American companies and institutions.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control, an intelligence and enforcement agency within the Department of the Treasury, also levied sanctions on First VPN administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi and Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev for selling tools used to disguise ransomware and other malware. These tools -- known as "cryptors" -- prevent security systems from detecting or deactivating them.

In May, European authorities dismantled First VPN, also known as 1VPNS, and arrested Rashevskyi, who is based in Dnipro, Ukraine, to culminate an investigation that began in 2021.

Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, said that First VPN was well publicized on Russian-language cybercrime forums as a service offering anonymous payments, hidden infrastructure and services "designed specifically for criminal use."

The agency also said the VPN service helped cybercriminals hide their identities while carrying out ransomware attacks and data theft, and that it appeared "in almost every major cybercrime investigation supported by Europol in recent years."

Representatives for the Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What is ransomware?

Ransomware is malicious software that gets into a computer system and prevents an individual or company from accessing files, systems or networks. The perpetrator will typically demand a ransom to regain access. It's a massive problem: One estimate puts the cost at $74 billion globally this year.

The FBI advises that people keep their operating systems and software programs updated, use anti-malware and antivirus programs and regularly back up data, among other tips. The FBI also does not recommend paying ransomware instigators.



Under the sanctions enacted this week, the Department of the Treasury will prohibit all transactions by people in the US involving property owned by Rashevskyi or Silayev. The department also said any of their property that is in the country or in possession of anyone in the country must be reported to the department. Financial institutions and others are prohibited from "engaging in certain transactions or activities" involving Rashevskyi or Silayev.

"The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior," the department said in the statement.

When used legally and ethically, a VPN is an invaluable tool for consumers seeking online privacy. The safest and most effective VPNs -- CNET advises against using free ones -- will not log or record your data, meaning that no one can see your internet activity. VPNs also mask your physical location by using a unique IP address, making it look as though you're in a different country than the one you're in. Many people use VPNs to watch online content that is geo-restricted from their actual country of residence.

But, as CNET's Attila Tomaschek writes, "total anonymity" is impossible, even with the best VPNs. They can help achieve some privacy, but so much of our data is accessible that a VPN can never give you "an all-encompassing invisibility cloak on the internet," he says.

Cybercrime forums and fake identities

In the news statement, the Department of the Treasury said Rashevskyi and First VPN began advertising their services in 2014 on various online cybercrime forums. First VPN said it did not log user identities or activities and would refuse to cooperate with law enforcement investigations into any possible illegal activity originating from servers it rents to customers.

The agency also said that Rashevskyi used fake identities to get companies to sell him infrastructure they would not have sold him if they had known his real identity. Internet service providers had complained about illegal activity emanating from First VPN servers, the statement said.

Ransomware criminals have used infrastructure obtained from First VPN to attack US businesses, financial services companies, hospitals and municipal governments, according to the Department of the Treasury.

Silayev, a Belarusian national, supplied encryption and obfuscation services to ransomware operators targeting US and allied entities, the Department of the Treasury said. These cryptors make malware look like harmless files, fooling the computer systems of companies and other institutions.
